subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: turning the problem into a game [Revision]
passage: Two hours into the power cut Leela had sighed thirty times, and Deepak had kicked the sofa twice. Rain drummed on the window, so going out was no use. "This is the worst evening," Deepak said. Then the torch beam slid across the wall and Leela's fingers moved without thinking. A rabbit. "Deepak, look." He frowned, then made a dog with his hand, and the dog chased the rabbit. A crocodile joined, then a giant bird, and they invented a story about a rabbit crossing a river with mangoes for a sleeping king. Amma looked in from the kitchen and stayed, holding her tea, to watch the crocodile. When the lights returned, both groaned. "Switch it off," said Deepak. "We are not finished."

qa.q: What animal did Leela make first with her hands in the torch beam?
What was Deepak feeling at the start of the evening?
qa.a: Bored and cross, as shown when he kicked the sofa and called it the worst evening.

qa.q: What other approach could the siblings try if the power cut lasted even longer?
qa.a: They could play a guessing game or sing, because those also need no electricity and keep them busy together. 😊

qa.q: How might Amma see the siblings' game after such a restless start?
qa.a: With relief and warmth, since she stayed in the doorway with her tea to watch instead of leaving.

grounding: Two siblings turn a dull evening without electricity into shadow puppets and a made-up story.

passage: The power in their Kolkata lane went at six, and the electricity office said it would be back "late night". By seven Arnab and his brother Raghav had fought twice over the one torch and once over nothing. "This is the worst evening ever," Raghav said. Arnab, lying on the floor, pointed the torch at the ceiling and saw his hand throw a huge shadow. He curled two fingers. A dog's head appeared on the wall. Raghav stopped sulking. "Do a crocodile." Within half an hour they had hung a white bedsheet from the cupboard and were making up a story about a dog who stole a crocodile's lunch. Their grandmother came to watch with her tea. When the lights came back at eleven, Raghav groaned. "Already?"

qa.q: When did the lights come back?
How did Raghav's feelings change during the evening?
qa.a: From sulky and frustrated to delighted, so much that he groaned when the lights returned.

qa.q: What else could the brothers try on the next power cut?
qa.a: Keep a torch each and plan a new shadow story, so there's less to fight over from the start.

qa.q: What was the evening like for their grandmother?
qa.a: She came with her tea to watch the show and seemed to enjoy it. 😊

grounding: During a long power cut, two brothers turn their frustration into a shadow-puppet story that becomes a happy memory.

passage:
"Didi, I'm bored. When is the light coming?"
"Nobody knows, Sachin. Maybe ten."
"It's only seven! I can't read, I can't watch anything, it's hot..."
"You've said 'hot' eleven times."
"Because it's hot!"
Nandini sighed and switched on the torch. The beam hit the wall. She hooked her thumbs together and flapped her fingers. "Look."
"A bird!"
"A crow. And the crow is very hungry." She made its beak open and shut. "Caw. Where is Sachin's dinner?"
Sachin giggled. "Let me do one!" He made a lumpy shape. "It's a... rabbit?"
"It's a potato with ears."
"The potato is scared of the crow!"
By the time Amma called them for dinner, the crow and the potato were best friends and had fought off a cat.

qa.q: How many times had Sachin said 'hot'?
How was Nandini feeling before she switched on the torch?
qa.a: Tired and irritated by the complaints, as her sigh shows.

qa.q: What else could the siblings do if the torch battery runs low?
qa.a: Tell stories in the dark or play a word game, which needs no light at all.

qa.q: How does the evening change for Sachin?
qa.a: From bored and hot to giggling and inventing his own shadow characters.

grounding: During a power cut, siblings turn a bored, hot evening into a shadow-puppet game with a torch.
